citation: Skaramagkas, Vasileios, Giorgos Giannakakis, Emmanouil Ktistakis, Dimitris Manousos, Ioannis Karatzanis, Nikolaos S. Tachos, Evanthia Tripoliti, Kostas Marias, Dimitrios I. Fotiadis, and Manolis Tsiknakis. "Review of Eye Tracking Metrics Involved in Emotional and Cognitive Processes." Preprint, v3, n.d. Journal/DOI not stated in the extracted text; internal citation evidence (most recent cited works dated 2020) places composition circa 2020-2021. Author affiliations: Institute of Computer Science, Foundation for Research and Technology Hellas (FORTH), Heraklion, Crete, Greece; Hellenic Mediterranean University; University of Crete; Institute of Molecular Biology and Biotechnology, FORTH, Ioannina; University of Ioannina. Acknowledges H2020 SeeFar project funding (GA No 826429).
discipline: biomedical signal processing / affective computing / eye-tracking methodology -- a comprehensive literature review (not an original experiment) of eye- and pupil-behaviour metrics for visual attention, emotional arousal, and cognitive workload detection
thesis: The authors identify a gap parallel to, but broader than, the boredom-specific literature elsewhere in this cluster: eye and pupil behaviour, though mediated by the autonomic nervous system just as biosignals are, has remained comparatively neglected relative to EEG/EDA/ECG research. The review's three stated aims are to (1) identify eye/pupil metrics significantly related to visual attention, emotional arousal, and cognitive workload; (2) determine efficient recognition methods based on those metrics; and (3) specify the most robust combined feature set for multimodal approaches. The authors state explicitly that no single eye feature discriminates cleanly among the three target processes, motivating a comprehensive survey restricted to studies of urban/daily-life activities (driving, reading, PC use) rather than laboratory-only paradigms. Notably, the text never uses the word 'boredom,' nor 'mind-wandering,' 'monotony,' or any Heideggerian vocabulary -- its cluster contribution is almost entirely instrumental (an atlas of eye-tracking measures) rather than construct-theoretic.

sections.title: Abstract / Index Terms
sections.summary: Previews an eye/pupil-metrics review oriented toward visual attention, emotional arousal, and cognitive workload, plus recognition methods, multimodal approaches, and public datasets.

sections.title: I. Introduction
sections.summary: Motivates the gap (eye/pupil behaviour under-researched relative to biosignals); states three review aims; previews Sections II-VII; restricts scope to urban/daily-life-activity studies.

sections.title: II. Emotional and Cognitive Processes
sections.summary: A. Visual attention (Underwood's selective-isolation definition); B. Emotional arousal and stress (Russell's circumplex model; arousal as global dynamism/lethargy); C. Cognitive workload (Sweller's cognitive load theory -- intrinsic/extraneous/germane load; Wierwille & Eggemeier's performance/subjective/physiological measurement taxonomy).

sections.title: III. Features Representing Eye and Pupil Behaviour
sections.summary: A. Visual fixations; B. Saccades; C. Microsaccades; D. Smooth pursuit eye movements; E. Pupil (mechanism plus a dedicated reliability-limitations discussion: illumination, humidity/temperature, age, camera angle); F. Eye blinks.

sections.title: IV. Video-based Eye and Pupil Tracking Systems and Methods
sections.summary: A. Video-based eye tracking (contrasted with EOG, photo/videooculography, scleral coil); B. Eye gaze estimation (2D regression, 3D model-based, cross-ratio, calibration-free methods); C. Estimation of pupil area (thresholding, dual-state open/closed models, CNN segmentation).

sections.title: V. Eye and Pupil Behaviour Metrics
sections.summary: The review's empirical core. A. Metrics related to visual attention (fixations, saccades/microsaccades/smooth pursuit, blinks, pupil; Table I). B. Metrics related to emotional arousal and stress (same structure; Table II). C. Metrics related to cognitive workload (same structure; Table III).

sections.title: VI. Multimodal Emotional and Cognitive Processes Recognition Methods
sections.summary: A. Emotional arousal recognition; B. Cognitive workload recognition; both organized around a single machine-learning comparison (Table IV, ~14 cited classifier studies, SVM/RF/NB/DT/AdaBoost/GMM/kNN/ANN/DBN).

sections.title: VII. Eye Behaviour Related Datasets
sections.summary: Surveys roughly a dozen public datasets (Table V) by subject count, stimuli, task, and included eye features; notes only 2 of ~14 datasets include pupil diameter and only 1 includes blink features.

sections.title: VIII. Discussion
sections.summary: Synthesizes findings per process (pupil+blink for arousal; fixations for attention; pupil+fixation+saccadic velocity for workload); names an explicit cross-process discrimination research gap; calls for a dataset spanning all three processes.

sections.title: Acknowledgment / References
sections.summary: H2020 SeeFar project funding (GA No 826429); 212 references, including several self-citations to co-author Giannakakis's prior stress-detection work.

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: genuine kinship via the review's own 'visual attention' construct, operationalized with the same metric vocabulary (fixation/gaze/blink-based disengagement) boredom researchers use elsewhere in this cluster; the review's object is general attention, not boredom-specific disengagement

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: not named; every process surveyed (arousal, workload, attention) is measured as a momentary, stimulus-or-task-bound condition within single sessions, a structural analogue to state-boredom framing found elsewhere in the cluster

constructs.label: mind-wandering / task-unrelated thought
constructs.treatment: not named; the scan-path/saliency/center-bias literature implicitly defines the on-task visual-engagement baseline against which mind-wandering-driven gaze deviation would register

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: single incidental mention only -- blink-rate decrease linked to 'attentional engagement and mental workload' (Maffei & Angrilli 2019); no independent theorization of flow or engagement

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: not named as such; an adjacent 'habituation effect' finding is reported (average pupil size rose specifically on first exposure to a repeated in-vehicle-information-system condition), physiologically adjacent to but not equivalent to monotony

constructs.label: profound/deep boredom (FCM 3rd form)
constructs.treatment: not treated -- no Heideggerian vocabulary anywhere in the source

measures.label: pupil dilation / pupillometry
measures.signal: pupil diameter/area variation, governed by sympathetic/parasympathetic antagonism
measures.apparatus: video-based IR/NIR eye trackers; pupil-area estimation via thresholding, dual-state open/closed eye models (Tian et al.), and CNN-based segmentation
measures.sampleN: review-level; aggregates dozens of cited studies, each with its own N (no single review-level N)
measures.keyResult: most-cited single ML classification feature (Table IV, present in nearly every classifier surveyed); most consistent single indicator of emotional arousal (Table II); positive correlate of cognitive workload (Table III); flagged reliability confounds -- illumination, ambient humidity/temperature, age-related baseline reduction, camera position/angle

measures.label: gaze variance / fixation dispersion
measures.signal: 2D/3D gaze coordinates; fixation count/duration/density/AOI metrics; saccade amplitude/velocity/rate; microsaccade rate/amplitude; smooth pursuit gain; Krejtz et al.'s coefficient K (focal vs. ambient scanning)
measures.apparatus: video-based eye trackers (head-mounted, desktop, mobile); EOG (historical); 2D-regression, 3D-model-based, and cross-ratio gaze-estimation algorithms
measures.sampleN: review-level; aggregates dozens of cited studies
measures.keyResult: fixation number, fixation duration, and total fixation time are the most robust (p<.01) indicators of visual attention (Table I); the 'basic' feature layer present in nearly every public dataset surveyed (Table V), though usually as 2D gaze points alone

measures.label: blink / eye-closure
measures.signal: blink rate (blinks/min); blink duration (0.1-0.4 sec average); Percentage of Eyelid Closure (PERCLOS); Average Eye Closure Speed (AECS)
measures.apparatus: same video-based trackers, applied to eyelid-closure detection
measures.keyResult: decreases with visual-attention focus (Table I); increases with emotional arousal/stress via blink duration (Table II); non-monotonic relation to cognitive workload -- decreases from low to medium load then plateaus (Table III); second-most-used ML feature after pupil diameter (Table IV); present in only 1 of ~14 surveyed public datasets (EGTEA Gaze+)

measures.label: heart rate / HRV
measures.apparatus: companion biosignal only -- not the review's own eye-based instrumentation; featured in several Table IV multimodal classifiers and the MAMEM Phase I dataset (GSR + heart rate)
measures.keyResult: combining heart rate/HRV with eye features substantially boosts multiclass classification accuracy relative to eye-only feature sets (part of the ~10-percentage-point average gain reported in Table IV)

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.signal: not the review's own primary data type -- framed categorically as one of three canonical cognitive-workload measurement types (performance / subjective / physiological)
measures.apparatus: n/a -- conceptual taxonomy (Wierwille & Eggemeier 1993), not an instrument this review itself deploys
measures.keyResult: no independent validation of self-report against eye metrics is attempted within this review, unlike the explicit null-correlation finding in this cluster's bor-sec-28 (Kim et al.)

measures.label: behavioral (RT / errors / performance-monitoring)
measures.signal: task performance metrics (number of errors, task completion measures)
measures.apparatus: 'performance measurements,' one of three canonical workload-measurement types (Wierwille & Eggemeier 1993)
measures.keyResult: concrete instance: blink duration and pupil dilation correlate strongly with number of errors in a high-cognitive-load arithmetic task (Borys et al., cited repeatedly across Sections V-C and Table III)

measures.label: ML classification
measures.signal: supervised classification of emotional-arousal or cognitive-workload state/level from eye-feature (and, in most studies, biosignal) feature vectors
measures.apparatus: SVM (dominant), Random Forest, Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, AdaBoost, Bagging Trees, Gaussian Mixture Models, k-NN, ANN, Deep Belief Network -- across ~14 cited studies (Table IV)
measures.sampleN: aggregated across cited studies; individual study Ns range roughly 4-60
measures.keyResult: eye-only classifiers average 71.5% accuracy for emotional arousal (best 93%, binary depression detection via blink metrics alone) and 78.64% for cognitive workload (best 99.5%); eye+biosignal classifiers average 81.76% (emotion) and 87.55% (workload) -- roughly a ten-percentage-point gain from adding biosignals, chiefly EEG

measures.label: EEG frontal alpha asymmetry / EEG alpha-theta power / EEG functional connectivity / EEG eyes-open vs. eyes-closed
measures.signal: not treated at all, even generically
measures.apparatus: EEG appears only as an undifferentiated companion 'biosignal' column in Table IV and the MAMEM Phase I dataset description
measures.keyResult: zero band-specific, frontal-asymmetry, functional-connectivity, or eyes-open/closed analysis anywhere in the text -- confirms this review's fit as an eye/pupil-metrics survey rather than an EEG-methods review

measures.label: predictive-processing model
measures.keyResult: the only 'predictive' term in the source is 'predictive smooth pursuit eye movements' (Kowler et al., cited at [28]), an anticipatory-tracking oculomotor phenomenon unrelated to the free-energy/active-inference predictive-processing theory used elsewhere in this cluster (e.g., bor-sec-20, Darling 2023) -- flagged explicitly to avoid a false-positive match

readings.claim: Fixation number, fixation duration, and total fixation time are the most robust and consistently significant (p<.01) indicators of increased visual attention across the cited literature; saccade amplitude and microsaccade rate are also useful, while pupil size shows only scattered involvement.

Pupil size increase is the most common single indicator for detecting emotional arousal across the cited literature, but the authors caution that detecting -- let alone quantifying -- arousal from pupil diameter alone is questionable.

Unlike emotional arousal, cognitive workload shows a wider variety of reliably involved eye metrics: fixation number, saccadic velocity, saccade rate, microsaccade amplitude, and pupil size increase with workload, while fixation duration, blink rate/duration, and microsaccade rate decrease.

Eye-feature-only classifiers average 71.5% accuracy for emotional-arousal discrimination (best 93%) and 78.64% for cognitive-workload discrimination (best 99.5%); adding biosignals (chiefly EEG) raises average accuracy by roughly ten percentage points in both domains, with SVM the most frequent best-performing classifier.

The vast majority of public eye-behaviour datasets provide only 2D gaze coordinates; only two of the surveyed datasets include pupil diameter and only one includes blink-related features; no dataset spans all three target processes (visual attention, emotional arousal, cognitive workload) simultaneously.

None of the surveyed studies attempts joint discrimination between emotional and cognitive processes (as opposed to levels within a single process), and the generalizability of reported classification results is limited by small, heterogeneous samples and tasks.

Pupil metrics carry significant reliability confounds -- sensitivity to illumination, ambient humidity/temperature, age-related baseline reduction, and camera position/angle -- that researchers should control for via centered stimuli and normal-state baselining.

interlocutors.name: Bradley, M.M., Miccoli, L., Escrig, M.A., & Lang, P.J. (2008)
interlocutors.role: pupil as a measure of emotional arousal and autonomic activation, cited in grounding the pupil-arousal link

interlocutors.name: Sweller, John (1994)
interlocutors.role: Cognitive Load Theory -- intrinsic/extraneous/germane load, structuring the review's cognitive-workload definition

interlocutors.name: Krejtz, Katarzyna; Duchowski, Andrew T.; et al.
interlocutors.role: coefficient K (focal/ambient attention metric) and pupil-diameter cognitive-load metrics, cited across visual-attention and workload sections

interlocutors.name: Eckstein, M.K., Guerra-Carrillo, B., Miller Singley, A.T., & Bunge, S.A. (2017) -- Beyond Eye Gaze
interlocutors.role: broader review of what eye-tracking reveals about cognition and cognitive development, cited in the Introduction's gap-statement

interlocutors.name: Giannakakis, G., Grigoriadis, D., Giannakaki, K., Simantiraki, O., Roniotis, A., & Tsiknakis, M. (2019)
interlocutors.role: self-citation -- co-author Giannakakis's own review on psychological stress detection using biosignals, cited to justify EEG's role as the strongest biosignal supplement to eye features

interlocutors.name: Maffei, A., & Angrilli, A. (2019)
interlocutors.role: spontaneous blink rate as an index of attention and emotion during film-clip viewing -- the source's single explicit link between blink rate and 'attentional engagement'

interlocutors.name: Holmqvist, Kenneth, & Blignaut, P. (2020) -- Small eye movements cannot be reliably measured by video-based P-CR eye-trackers
interlocutors.role: video-based eye-tracker measurement-error limitation, cited in Section IV-A; same lead author as this cluster's bor-sec-36 (Holmqvist et al., Eye Tracking: Empirical Foundations for a Minimal Reporting Guideline) -- a different paper, verified same-author match, not the identical work

interlocutors.role: eye-tracking study of automatic visual attention to sensual imagery, discussed in Section V-A1 (~p.6); same author group (Cheval/Boisgontier) as this cluster's bor-sec-34 (Cheval et al., Physically Active Individuals Look for More) -- a different paper, verified same-author-group match, not the identical work

interlocutors.name: Wierwille, W.W., & Eggemeier, F.T. (1993)
interlocutors.role: performance/subjective/physiological taxonomy of cognitive-workload measurement types, structuring Section II-C

tensions.axis: salience-based/bottom-up computational models of visual attention vs. observed natural-task eye-movement behaviour
tensions.note: the review notes that salience-based schemes, though widely used computationally, 'prove to be poor in predicting eye movement behaviour in natural tasks' -- a tension it surfaces without resolving.

tensions.axis: single-modality (eye-only) vs. multimodal (eye+biosignal) classification accuracy ceiling
tensions.note: eye-only classifiers plateau around 71.5-78.64% average accuracy across the cited studies, while adding biosignals (chiefly EEG) raises averages to 81.76-87.55% -- the review treats this as an open design tradeoff rather than adjudicating a single best pipeline.

tensions.axis: pupil size as a convenient, near-universal single indicator vs. its serious methodological reliability confounds
tensions.note: the review flags illumination, humidity/temperature, age, and camera-angle confounds explicitly, cautioning against uncritical reliance on pupil-only measures even though pupil diameter is the most-cited single ML feature across the surveyed literature.

tensions.axis: absence of any public dataset spanning all three target processes (visual attention, emotional arousal, cognitive workload) simultaneously
tensions.note: explicitly named as an open data-availability gap and a call for future dataset construction.

dataset_channels.target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study) -- pupillometry channel
dataset_channels.note: The review's Section III-E/V-A4/B4/C4/Table IV treatment of pupil dilation as the single most-used eye-based metric across visual-attention, emotional-arousal, and cognitive-workload classification offers a plausible methodological template for a future VR attention study's pupillometry channel, but its own apparatus discussion (Section IV) is screen- or head-mounted-glasses-based, not integrated-VR-headset eye tracking, so hardware fit is unconfirmed until the dataset entry specifies its own instrumentation (P/anticipatory-application).

dataset_channels.target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study) -- gaze variance / fixation-dispersion channel
dataset_channels.note: The review's fixation/saccade/microsaccade/smooth-pursuit metric taxonomy (Section III-A-D, Table I) and its gaze-estimation methods survey (Section IV-B) offer a plausible methodological menu for a future VR attention study's gaze channel, but VR-headset-integrated eye tracking differs substantially in geometry (3D gaze vectors, headset-relative AOIs) from the 2D screen-based paradigms this review surveys; linkage requires the dataset entry's own instrumentation to be confirmed (P/anticipatory-application).

dataset_channels.target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study) -- blink / eye-closure channel
dataset_channels.note: The review's blink-rate/blink-duration/PERCLOS/AECS treatment (Section III-F, Table IV) offers a plausible methodological template for a future VR attention study's blink channel, though the review itself notes only 1 of ~14 surveyed public datasets includes blink features at all, underscoring how rarely this channel is actually instrumented even in non-VR eye-tracking research (P/anticipatory-application).
